courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology · Unit F172: Genetics (Topic Area 3 / NEA Task 2)
ocrSpec: Topic Area 3.1.2 (4 Lab Test Classes) + 3.2.1 (Adult Tests) + 3.2.2 (Prenatal & Newborn) + 3.2.3 (IVF & Preimplantation Testing)
focus: Selecting & Explaining Appropriate Molecular Diagnostic Testing for Huntington's Disease (P12) and Analysing the Role of Adult, Prenatal, Newborn & Preimplantation Genetic Tests Across Ben's Family Context (M7)
deliverable: 75-minute classroom deck covering all 4 OCR lab test categories (molecular, chromosomal, gene expression, biochemical), adult/prenatal/newborn/IVF-PGD pathways, and a full P12 molecular justification + M7 family-wide testing analysis for Ben's case study.

objectives.knowledge: Compare molecular, chromosomal, gene expression, and biochemical genetic tests (3.1.2) and explain why targeted molecular PCR CAG-repeat sizing is appropriate to diagnose Huntington's disease (P12).
objectives.application: Differentiate adult genetic tests (diagnostic, predictive, ancestry), embryo/baby tests (prenatal CVS/amniocentesis, newborn heel-prick screening & regional differences), and IVF preimplantation genetic testing (3.2.1–3.2.3).
objectives.evaluation: Analyse the clinical role, timing, advantages, limitations, and suitability of each testing modality across Ben's entire family context (Ben, pregnant wife/unborn fetus, 6yo & 3yo children, future pregnancies) (M7).

terminology.def: Laboratory assay amplifying DNA from a blood/saliva sample (specifically exon 1 of HTT) and using capillary fragment sizing to count exact CAG trinucleotide repeats.

Diagnostic testing confirms a genetic cause in a symptomatic patient (Ben); predictive (presymptomatic) testing detects mutation status in an asymptomatic at-risk relative (deferred until age 18 for HD).
Invasive fetal sampling during pregnancy — Chorionic Villus Sampling (11–14 weeks) or Amniocentesis (15–20 weeks) — to test fetal DNA, carrying ~0.5–1% miscarriage risk.
Universal heel-prick test at day 5 of life (most common genetic test globally) targeting actionable early-onset conditions (e.g. PKU, CF, SCD); NOT used for adult-onset HD.
Testing biopsied blastomere/trophectoderm cells from IVF embryos prior to uterine transfer so only unaffected (hh) embryos are implanted.

theoryPoints: Four Laboratory Test Categories (Spec 3.1.2 — P12): Molecular (DNA sequence/repeat mutations via PCR/sequencing — SELECTED for HD), Chromosomal (karyotyping/FISH for large numerical/structural anomalies like Trisomy 21 — CANNOT see tiny CAG expansions), Gene Expression (mRNA levels in tissues e.g. cancer panels), Biochemical (enzyme/protein metabolite activity e.g. PKU phenylalanine — cannot reliably diagnose pre/early HD).

Molecular Diagnosis of HD (P12): Peripheral blood EDTA sample → genomic DNA extraction → targeted PCR / triplet-primed PCR across HTT exon 1 → capillary electrophoresis fragment sizing reporting exact CAG repeat count (≤26 normal, 27–35 intermediate/mutable, 36–39 reduced penetrance, ≥40 full penetrance).

Adult, Embryo, Newborn & IVF Pathways (Spec 3.2.1–3.2.3): Adult tests (diagnostic vs predictive vs direct-to-consumer ancestry); Prenatal tests (invasive CVS 11–14 wks, amniocentesis 15–20 wks, plus non-invasive NIPT context); Newborn screening (why most common: universal NHS heel-prick for immediately treatable conditions; regional/international variation driven by population allele prevalence, cost & healthcare infrastructure); IVF + PGD/PGT-M (ovarian stimulation → egg retrieval → fertilisation → embryo biopsy → molecular PCR screening → transfer of hh embryo).

Analytical Mapping to Ben's Case Study Context (M7 — Whole Family): (1) Symptomatic Ben → Confirmatory Molecular Diagnostic Test (essential to confirm HD over mimics, access specialist care, quantify CAG length); (2) 6yo daughter & 3yo son → Predictive Testing DEFERRED until age 18 (no childhood treatment; protects autonomy); (3) Unborn 3rd child → Prenatal CVS/amniocentesis (direct or exclusion testing) weighed against miscarriage risk and termination dilemmas; (4) Future pregnancies → IVF with PGD/PGT-M (prevents transmission without termination, but costly, invasive, ~30–40% cycle success); (5) Newborn screening & commercial ancestry kits → Clinically inappropriate for HD.

workedExample.title: Evaluating Why Molecular PCR Beats Other Tests (P12) & Mapping Ben's Family (M7)
workedExample.subtitle: From Pass-level test selection to Merit-level analytical comparison

steps.label: Step 1 — P12 Justification (Why Molecular PCR?)
steps.detail: Compare all 4 OCR test classes: karyotyping lacks resolution to detect a ~120 bp CAG expansion on chromosome 4; biochemical and gene-expression assays do not measure repeat count. Targeted PCR + fragment sizing directly measures exact CAG length from a routine blood draw with >99% analytical accuracy.

steps.label: Step 2 — M7 Analysis: Symptomatic vs Asymptomatic Family
steps.detail: Contrast Ben's diagnostic test (confirms chorea aetiology immediately) against predictive testing for his 6yo and 3yo children (clinically inappropriate in minors because no childhood preventative therapy exists and a positive result removes their future autonomous choice).

steps.label: Step 3 — M7 Analysis: Reproductive Pathways (Prenatal vs PGD)
steps.detail: Analyse Ben and his wife's options for the current pregnancy (invasive CVS/amniocentesis: definitive fetal status but 0.5–1% miscarriage risk and emotionally agonising termination decision) versus IVF + PGD for any future child (avoids termination and prevents transmission, but requires NHS HFEA eligibility/funding, hormonal stimulation, and carries lower live-birth rates).

hingeQuestions.question: Why is chromosomal karyotyping unsuitable for diagnosing Ben's Huntington's disease compared to a molecular genetic test (P12)?
options: Karyotyping can only be performed on plant cells
Karyotyping only visualises whole chromosomes and large structural rearrangements (millions of bp), so it cannot detect a sub-microscopic trinucleotide CAG repeat expansion within exon 1 of HTT
Karyotyping destroys all DNA before PCR can begin
Huntington's disease is caused by an extra whole chromosome 4 (trisomy 4)
hingeQuestions.explanation: HD is a single-gene trinucleotide repeat expansion (~120+ bp in exon 1 of HTT), far below the megabase microscopic resolution of a chromosomal karyotype; targeted molecular PCR fragment analysis is required.

hingeQuestions.question: Why is newborn blood-spot screening the most common form of genetic testing in the UK, yet NOT used to screen newborns for Huntington's disease (M7)?
options: Newborn heel-prick blood contains no white blood cells or DNA

Newborn screening is universal because it detects treatable early-onset conditions (e.g. PKU, MCADD, sickle cell) where immediate intervention prevents severe disability/death — whereas HD is adult-onset with no childhood preventative treatment
Because UK law bans all genetic testing of babies under 1 year old
Because HD only occurs outside the United Kingdom
hingeQuestions.explanation: Newborn screening follows Wilson & Jungner principles: screening universally only for conditions where early presymptomatic treatment meaningfully improves childhood outcomes. HD fails this criterion and violates the child's future autonomy.

plenary: P12 mastery: Justify targeted molecular testing (PCR + CAG repeat fragment sizing on chromosome 4) by directly contrasting it against chromosomal, gene expression, and biochemical tests.
Topic Area 3.2 mastery: Clearly separate adult (diagnostic, predictive, ancestry), embryo/baby (prenatal CVS/amniocentesis, universal newborn screening & regional differences), and IVF/PGD pathways.

M7 mastery: Analyse every testing pathway in Ben's family context — why diagnostic testing helps Ben now, why predictive testing is deferred for his children, and the trade-offs of prenatal testing vs IVF-PGD.
